extracted.intended_audience: students of journalism and young newspaper reporters
extracted.subtask_description: Practical rules and analytic checklist for writing and judging newspaper news stories, including principles of news selection, structure (leads and body), style (paragraphs, sentences, diction), types of stories, sources/methods, and typographical conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposes of newspaper content (classification of contents)
rubrics_metrics.description: The average daily newspaper includes a larger amount and variety of reading matter and its contents may be grouped in seven classes: (1) news stories; (2) special feature articles; (3) editorials; (4) dramatic, musical, and literary criticism; (5) practical advice and useful information; (6) humorous matter; (7) fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Of these, news stories, special feature articles, editorials, and dramatic/musical/literary criticism are considered distinctly journalistic. Understand which class a piece belongs to because purpose and treatment differ (e.g., editorials interpret and persuade; features elaborate or entertain).

rubrics_metrics.name: News values
rubrics_metrics.description: News is anything timely that interests a number of readers; the best news has the greatest interest for the greatest number. News values are based largely on the reader's interest in (1) timely matters, (2) extraordinary events and circumstances, (3) struggles for supremacy (politics, business, sports), (4) matters involving property, life, and welfare, (5) children, (6) animals, (7) hobbies and amusements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Degree of interest depends on reader familiarity with persons/places/things involved, their importance/prominence, and closeness of relation to reader's personal affairs. Local interest usually > general interest; give local ends to telegraph/general news to increase local relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of news stories (informative vs feature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two general types: (1) informative news story — chief aim is to give the facts of the news; (2) feature or human interest story — chief aim is to take material of little or no news value and make it interesting. Informative stories may be purely factual or constructive (intend wholesome effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feature stories test literary ability and may adopt devices of fiction; distinguish between using fiction's methods to portray events faithfully and inventing fictitious details (forbidden). Length is determined by value or ability to sustain interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary lead requirements (Who? What? Where? When? Why? How?)
rubrics_metrics.description: The informative story usually begins with a summary lead that answers the reader's questions Who? What? Where? When? Why? How?. The summary lead includes: (1) persons, (2) event, (3) place, (4) time, (5) cause, (6) significant circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any one element may be 'featured' in the place of prominence at the beginning of the story. Entertaining/feature stories often avoid summary leads and may begin as a short story would.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body arrangement and repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: In the body, details follow a logical order; in narrative stories arrangement is usually chronological. Only such of the details summarized in the lead are repeated in the body as are needed for clearness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Round out stories in the last paragraph if possible, but endings are less crucial because copy may be cut in make-up. Avoid unnecessary repetition; paragraphs should be closely connected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness
rubrics_metrics.description: Conciseness requires that needless words be omitted, that only such details be given as are necessary for effective presentation, and that the length of the story be proportionate to the importance of the material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Boil it down' and 'Cut it to the bone' are constant admonitions; conciseness is necessary but does not require bald, unattractive prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearness and simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearness is secured by comparative simplicity of diction, of sentence construction, and of paragraph structure; newspaper style should be comparatively simple and avoid learned diction, elaborate figures, and involved sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write for rapid reading and for readers of limited education as well as the well-educated. Explain technical/scientific words when used; avoid slang unless tone justifies it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readability and emphasis (positioning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Important details are placed at the beginning of paragraphs and sentences where they will catch the eye at once; emphasis by initial position is distinctive of newspaper writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This leads to loose (not periodic) sentence structure, short paragraphs, and arrangement designed for rapid scanning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of good news writing
rubrics_metrics.description: News writing should be (1) concise, (2) clear, (3) comparatively simple, (4) easily read, and (5) attractive to all classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for clearness, force, animation, humor, pathos, and taste appropriate to subject and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding fictionalization and dishonest embellishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Embellishment of news stories with fictitious details to make them more interesting, and the distortion or suppression of significant facts to accomplish an end, are opposed to the fundamental purpose of the newspaper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using devices of fiction to portray events faithfully is permitted; inventing facts or substituting fictitious details to heighten effect is forbidden. Some examples with imaginary details may be used only for discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive vs destructive treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Informative stories may be treated purely as records or arranged to produce a wholesome/constructive effect on readers — e.g., emphasizing causes/responsibility to prevent recurrence — or they may be sensational and encourage imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporter should consider influence of coverage; avoid making wrongdoing attractive. Newspapers may choose mirror-like impartiality, constructive emphasis, or sensational treatment — each has ethical implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of news and attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: News sources include public and private records, reports, officials, eye-witnesses, and these should be inferred or cited; a list of sources is helpful to beginners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note sources carefully to permit verification and to be able to draw on the same types of sources for similar stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of news gathering and evidence in copy
rubrics_metrics.description: The story should show how details were obtained — e.g., interview questions inferred from replies, circumstances under which material was secured, use of officials/records/eye-witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should note hints about methods in examples and question whether the reporter failed to get important details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type of discourse (narrative, descriptive, expository)
rubrics_metrics.description: News stories in method are narrative, descriptive, expository, or any combination; narrative often chronological, description may be suggestive or detailed, exposition explains motives/causes/results and should be simple and lucid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose mix of forms suited to the material; long stories permit fuller description, short ones require suggestive touches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure analysis checklist (lead & body)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze beginning (summary lead or unconventional beginning) and body: does lead contain essential facts concisely; is most striking detail featured in opening words; is lead proportionate in length; how are details arranged in body?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for evidence of copy cut in make-up, paragraph connection, unnecessary repetition, and alternative elements that might have been featured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary style elements (paragraphs, sentences, words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze paragraph length, sentence length, unity of thought, coherence, and emphasis. Typical newspaper paragraph contains 35–75 words (about half as long as book prose). Involved constructions and long periodic sentences have no place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer specific words in original combinations over colorless general terms and trite phrases. Avoid technical jargon unless explained; slang and colloquial expressions permissible when justified by tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typographical style and consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Typographical details — abbreviation, capitalization, hyphenation, use of numerals — vary by paper; consistency is essential. Special typographical devices (boxes, bold-face type) may be used to highlight significant facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note methods for lists (dead/injured), market reports, sports scores, and keep consistent house style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions affecting news writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing is done rapidly under pressure and with limited revision; narrow column widths require short paragraphs; the popular demand for novelty encourages new forms; newspapers must appeal to all classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept constraints (speed, space) but avoid slovenly English and stock phrases; adapt style to circulation and readers' education levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of human-interest and feature techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Informative stories may develop human interest; feature/human-interest stories are entertaining and use fiction methods. Using fiction's devices to portray events faithfully is commendable; substituting fictitious details is not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring out human-interest phases when they add effectiveness; in features, sustain reader interest — length depends on success in doing so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis framework (outline for evaluating stories)
rubrics_metrics.description: An explicit analytic checklist covering: NEWS VALUES (paper, policy, circulation, audience, source of interest, space justification), SOURCES OF NEWS (origin, records, consulted persons), METHODS OF GATHERING (evidence of methods, missing details), PURPOSE (fairness, suppression, constructive/destructive effect), TYPE OF STORY (inform/entertain, form, clarity, pace, use of quotations, description), STRUCTURE (lead type, essential facts, arrangement, cuts, paragraph connection, repetition), plus more detailed questions under each heading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the numbered questions provided to evaluate a story in class or editorial review. The checklist supplies concrete prompts for judging news value, sourcing, fairness, structure, and style.
